t: Maximum Product of the Length of Two Palindromic Subsequences: Bitmask Enumeration
o: Split the indices of s, whose length is at most 12, into three buckets: characters taken by the first palindromic subsequence, characters taken by the second, and characters unused by both, then maximize the product of the two lengths. In leetcodecom, choosing ete in one bucket and cdc in another yields 3 * 3 = 9; bb forces two singleton buckets worth 1 * 1 = 1; accbcaxxcxx achieves accca and xxcxx for 5 * 5 = 25. The tiny length is the whole story: there are only 3^12, about 531000, ways to assign indices to buckets, and any set of chosen indices is just a 12-bit mask.
k: With n at most 12, every index set is a mask among only 4096 possibilities per subsequence.
Disjointness of two subsequences is a single bitwise check: a AND b must be zero.
Precomputing whether each mask forms a palindrome costs O(2^n * n) once and pays off across all pairs.
Iterating submasks of the complement enumerates exactly the legal partners of each palindrome mask.

a.i: Each index has three destinies, first subsequence, second, or unused, giving 3^n assignments reachable by straightforward recursion. At each leaf, test both accumulated strings for palindromicity and update the best product when both are nonempty and valid. With n = 12 this explores around half a million leaves, which is fast enough.
s: Recurse over index i with the strings built so far for subsequences A and B.
Branch into appending s[i] to A, appending it to B, or skipping it.
At i = n, require both strings nonempty and palindromic.
Track the maximum product of their lengths across leaves.
a.t: O(3^n * n) since 3^12 is about 531441 paths with O(n) palindrome checks at each leaf.
a.sp: O(n) recursion depth plus the strings carried down the recursion.

a.n: Approach 2: Palindrome Masks + Complement Submask Pairing
a.i: Represent each candidate index set as a bitmask; two subsequences are compatible iff their masks are disjoint. Precompute for all 2^n masks whether the selected characters form a palindrome and how long they are. Then for each palindromic mask a, walk all submasks b of its complement using the classic b = (b-1) & comp trick and relax the answer with len[a] * len[b]; summing 2^popcount over complements gives exactly 3^n pair visits.
s: For every mask from 1 to 2^n - 1, record its popcount-style length and whether it spells a palindrome.
For each palindromic mask a compute rest = full XOR a as the pool of available indices.
Iterate every nonzero submask b of rest via b = (b - 1) & rest.
Whenever b is also palindromic, update the answer with length[a] * length[b].
a.t: O(2^n * n) for palindrome precomputation plus O(3^n) pairing, since the total count of complement submasks over all masks equals 3^n.
a.sp: O(2^n) for the per-mask length and palindrome tables.

w: Say the constraint out loud first: n at most 12 screams bitmask enumeration, so jump straight to Approach 2 after sketching the recursion. Pitfalls: letting both subsequences claim the same index (disjointness via AND), forgetting single-character subsequences are palindromes, which the bb case needs, and double-counting ordered pairs, avoided here because b only ranges over the complement of a. Follow-ups: maximize the sum instead of the product, or extend to three disjoint palindromic subsequences.
